questions.q: What is the first step in the controlling process according to NCERT, and why must standards be set in quantitative terms wherever possible?
questions.a: The first step is setting performance standards. Standards should be quantitative (e.g., "produce 5,000 units/day") because they make comparison with actual performance objective, precise, and easy. A wrong answer like "measuring actual performance" shows the student confuses sequence; saying "qualitative standards are better" reveals misunderstanding that qualitative standards (e.g., "improve morale") are harder to measure and compare.

questions.q: A manager measures actual performance only after the task is fully completed. According to the textbook, when should measurement ideally happen, and why?
questions.a: Measurement should happen during performance wherever possible (e.g., checking each part before assembly, continuous gas monitoring). This allows early detection and correction. A student who says "after completion" misses the textbook's emphasis on concurrent measurement for timely control; they confuse controlling with post-mortem inspection.

questions.q: In a manufacturing company, labour cost increased by 5% and postal charges increased by 15%. Using critical point control, which deviation should management focus on and why?
questions.a: Management should focus on the 5% labour cost increase because labour cost is a Key Result Area (KRA) critical to organisational success, while postal charges are insignificant. A student who picks the 15% postal increase fails to understand that critical point control prioritises impact on goals, not percentage magnitude. This is a classic board exam trap.

questions.q: Compare and contrast "Critical Point Control" and "Management by Exception". How do they work together in the analysing deviations step?
questions.a: Critical Point Control identifies Key Result Areas (KRAs) to monitor; Management by Exception states only deviations beyond permissible limits in those KRAs should be reported to top management. Together, they ensure managers focus time on significant deviations in critical areas. A student who says they are the same concept or that Management by Exception means ignoring small deviations in all areas (not just KRAs) shows incomplete analysis.

questions.q: A company sets a standard of 2% allowable defect rate. Actual defects are 2.5%. The production manager argues this is within acceptable limits because "it's close". Evaluate this argument using the controlling process principles.
questions.a: The argument is invalid. The controlling process requires pre-defined acceptable deviation ranges. If 2% is the standard, any deviation beyond it (even 0.1%) must be analysed and reported if it's a KRA. "Close" is subjective; control demands objectivity. A student who accepts the manager's view misunderstands that standards are benchmarks, not rough targets, and that analysing deviations requires adherence to pre-set limits.

questions.q: Create a real-world scenario (Indian context) where a service organisation uses all five steps of the controlling process. Include at least one qualitative standard and show how management by exception is applied.
questions.a: Example: A Bengaluru-based food delivery app sets standards: (1) Quantitative: 30-minute average delivery time; Qualitative: Customer satisfaction ≥ 4.5/5. (2) Measures actual: 35 min avg, 4.2 rating. (3) Compares: Both deviations negative. (4) Analyses: Uses critical point control — delivery time is KRA; satisfaction is secondary. Management by exception: Only delivery time deviation (>5 min beyond limit) escalated to CEO. (5) Corrective: Hires more delivery partners, optimises routing algorithm. A poor answer lacks qualitative standard, misses KRA focus, or doesn't show exception reporting.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Controlling is the systematic process of setting performance standards, measuring actual performance, comparing it with standards, analysing deviations, and taking corrective action to ensure ______ goals are achieved efficiently and effectively.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are the ______ manager at a textile factory in Surat.
What is Controlling? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Controlling is the systematic process of setting performance standards, measuring actual performance, comparing it with standards, analysing deviations, and taking corrective action to ensure organisational goals are achieved efficiently and effectively.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Controlling?
questions.a: Students often think "controlling" means only the last step (taking corrective action) or that it is a one-time event at the end of a period.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can list the five steps of the controlling process in correct sequence, explain the purpose of each step with a business example, and distinguish between critical point control and management by exception as tools for analysing deviations.
